source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd Study 1
finding: A crowd of 12 LLMs, aggregated by the median, matched a human crowd on 31 binary questions. It beat the 50% baseline.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs 0.25 baseline, t(30)=-2.35, p=0.026. Human crowd (925 forecasters) 0.19 (SD 0.19); difference t(60)=0.19, p=0.85. Equivalence within a medium effect bound.
limits: Only 31 questions. Aggregate was a plain median, no extremizing. Models were from 2023 and had no retrieval.
agent_relevance: Aggregating different models by median is a cheap and tested gain. This is cross-model diversity, not same-model resampling (G4).

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: single-model scores
finding: Individual models varied widely. Best single model (GPT-4) was already near the crowd. The median crowd protects against weak members.
numbers: Mean Brier: GPT-4 0.15, GPT-4+Bing 0.16, Bard 0.19, Claude 2 0.21, Mistral-7B 0.24, Llama-2-70B 0.25, Coral 0.38; human 0.19. ANOVA F(12,354)=2.64, p=0.002; only Coral differed after Tukey.
limits: Per-model SDs are large (0.11 to 0.40), so ranking is weak. The median crowd (0.20) did not beat the best single model (GPT-4, 0.15).
agent_relevance: A pooled crowd does not beat its best member. Pooling mainly buys robustness when you cannot tell which member is best.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) acquiescence bias in LLM forecasts
finding: Most models predicted above 50% although fewer than half of questions resolved yes. Median pooling still beat the baseline despite this shared bias.
numbers: Mean model predictions significantly above 50%; one raw forecast of 99.5% against a median of 60% is cited. Aggregate described as overconfident toward yes.
quote: wisdom of crowds' effect using median as our aggregation is able to counteract even this acquiescence bias
limits: Bias direction depends on the question mix (here under half resolved yes). Shared bias is not removed by pooling.
agent_relevance: Models share a yes-lean. Pooling samples of one model keeps that lean. Any push away from 0.5 would amplify it (G4).

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Study 2: LLMs see the human median
finding: Showing GPT-4 and Claude 2 the human median improved them 17 to 28%, but a plain average of machine and human median was better still.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier 0.17 to 0.14 (p=0.003). Plain machine-human average beat the models' own updates: GPT-4 0.13 (t(92)=2.58, p=0.011), Claude 2 0.14 (t(92)=3.53, p=0.001).
limits: Models moved toward the human median. Part of the gain is just agreement.
agent_relevance: When an outside estimate exists, averaging with it beats asking the model to revise. Keep averaging a mechanical step, not a prompt.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: A retrieval plus reasoning plus fine-tuned LLM system, ensembled by a trimmed mean, came close to the human crowd on a test set after the models' cutoffs.
numbers: Test Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 (random 0.250), accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. Weighted average of system and crowd (crowd 4x) 0.146. When crowd is between 0.3 and 0.7, crowd 0.240 vs system 0.237.
limits: Gap to crowd remains on average. Gains appear where crowd is uncertain.
agent_relevance: Hybrid average beat both parts. Value of an LLM is largest where the crowd is unsure.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) ensembling methods ablation
finding: Five aggregators on 6 base forecasts per question differed by almost nothing. The LLM-based aggregator (USC variant) was worse than no ensembling.
numbers: Validation Brier: mean 0.1656, median 0.1651, geometric mean 0.1655, trimmed mean 0.1649, USC 0.1691, no ensemble 0.1676, human crowd 0.1600.
limits: Trimmed mean here is non-standard (halve weight of the forecast farthest from the median). Differences are in the third decimal.
agent_relevance: The averaging rule matters little. Letting an LLM pool answers can hurt.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) calibration of the system
finding: The system was naturally well calibrated, and standard recalibration (binning, isotonic regression) did not help.
numbers: No numeric gain from binning or isotonic regression (paper states no improvement).
quote: standard calibration methods such as binning or isotonic regression do not improve performance
limits: Contrast with c15 where Platt scaling helped. Base models, retrieval and question sets differ.
agent_relevance: Whether pushing away from 0.5 helps depends on whether the base forecasts are under-confident. Measure first.

source: Schoenegger, Park et al. (2024) AI-Augmented Predictions: LLM assistants improve human forecasting
finding: Human forecasters with an LLM advice assistant were more accurate. The overconfident, base-rate-neglecting assistant helped almost as much as the good one.
numbers: N=991, six questions. Accuracy gain 24% to 28% over control. Without the outlier question 3: 41% for superforecasting assistant vs 29% for the noisy one. Mean-of-medians without Q3: 0.11 (superforecasting), 0.28 (noisy), 0.15 (control).
limits: One outlier item (bitcoin hash rate) changes the picture. Small question set.
agent_relevance: Advice from a model can shift a crowd, so inputs may stop being independent.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) does LLM advice hurt crowd aggregation
finding: Preregistered check whether shared LLM advice homogenizes the crowd and weakens aggregation. No consistent harm found; result mixed.
numbers: Aggregate accuracy not reduced by either assistant; noisy assistant improved aggregate in the preregistered test but was worse once Q3 was dropped (0.28 vs 0.15 control).
limits: Medians across 6 questions only. Authors say they cannot give the full effect.
agent_relevance: Direct test of the independence worry behind G4. Shared inputs did not clearly break pooling, but power was low.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: human vs LLM scores
finding: Superforecaster median beat the public median and every LLM on a dynamic benchmark. The top LLMs saw crowd values on market questions.
numbers: Overall Brier: superforecasters 0.096, public 0.121, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (with freeze values) 0.122. Best LLM without crowd access 0.136. Superforecasters vs GPT-4o gap 0.054.
limits: Humans forecast 200 questions only. Benchmark is updated, so numbers move.
agent_relevance: A ceiling reference: the expert crowd is still ahead of single LLM pipelines.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench LLM ensemble pooling rules
finding: An ensemble of 3 models times 3 superforecaster-written prompts (9 forecasts) was pooled several ways. Geometric rules were slightly best.
numbers: Brier: median 0.197, trimmed mean 0.197, geometric mean 0.194, geometric mean of log odds 0.194 (2 SE about 0.023 to 0.024).
limits: Differences are far inside the error bars. No extremizing step was tested.
agent_relevance: Pooling rule is second order. Pool across models and prompts, not repeated samples (G4).

source: Hsieh et al. (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Forecasting
finding: An ensemble of ReAct agents with tools matched human predictors. Ensembling helped agents but not raw base models.
numbers: Agent ensemble Brier 0.169 vs single agent 0.180; human 0.172. GPT-4o: ensemble 0.218 vs single 0.210 (worse). Ensemble SD: base LMs 0.150 vs ReAct 0.092. Calibration index 0.0194 (GPT-4o) vs 0.0129 (ReAct mean).
quote: Ensembles only contribute to the final performance if each ensemble member is already sufficiently calibrated.
limits: Small ensembles (size 3 to 4). One dataset.
agent_relevance: Ensembling only paid when each member was already calibrated and low variance.

source: Alur, Stadie, Kang et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: ensemble size and rule
finding: Ten independent runs of the same agent beat one run. Mean, median and trimmed mean were equal. Returns shrink after a handful of runs.
numbers: Brier (table 9): simple mean 0.1140, trimmed mean 0.1142, median 0.1138, single forecast 0.1182. Sharp drop from 1 to 5 forecasts and small gain from 5 to 15 (bootstrap from 50 per question).
limits: Same-model samples have correlated errors, which explains the shrinking returns.
agent_relevance: Averaging same-model runs fixes variance only. It does not fix shared bias (G4).

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: supervisor agent
finding: A supervisor that finds disagreements, searches to resolve them, and tags its confidence beat plain averaging. Best-of-k and a non-agentic LLM pooler did poorly.
numbers: Brier: agentic supervisor 0.1125, non-agentic 0.1168, best-of-k 0.1191, no synthesis 0.1199. Best-of-k picked a bottom-three forecast 7.2% of the time. Only high-confidence updates replaced the mean.
limits: Supervisor adds search cost. Gain over the mean is small.
agent_relevance: If an agent reconciles samples, it should act on the disagreement with new evidence, not vote or pick.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: Platt scaling and extremizing
finding: Pushing forecasts away from 0.5 improved Brier. Platt scaling on the mean was best. It equals log-odds extremizing of the geometric mean.
numbers: FB-7-21 Brier: Platt scaling 0.1076 (fixed coefficient), 0.1071 (leave-one-out trained), 0.1104 (trained on another benchmark); isotonic 0.1140. Biggest gains in the 0.2 to 0.4 and 0.6 to 0.8 bins. Coefficient sqrt(3), about 1.73; best fit 2.27 for the agent, 1.72 for superforecasters.
limits: Only helps if forecasts are on the right side of 0.5. Single benchmark family. The report writes the coefficient as 3 in places; the source theory gives sqrt(3).
agent_relevance: Strongest AI-side evidence that extremizing works on LLM forecasts, even from same-model samples. It cuts against G4 as worded, so G4 should say: no extremizing on vote counts, but a fitted or small fixed map on a pooled probability may be tested.

source: Alur et al. (2025) agent vs superforecasters under scaling
finding: Applying the same Platt coefficient to superforecasters is needed for a fair comparison. The agent beat them across coefficients.
numbers: At the superforecasters' best coefficient (1.72) the agent with fixed sqrt(3) scaling still scored better. Public survey median 0.1450 beat the mean 0.1586.
limits: Superforecaster coefficient is fit on the benchmark itself.
agent_relevance: Test extremizing as a post-hoc map fitted on held-out data.

source: Alur et al. (2025) blend with market price
finding: Where the market is better, a blend with the LLM still beats the market. Where the LLM is better, the market adds nothing.
numbers: FB-Market: agent 0.075 (weight 0.87), market 0.097, blend 0.079. MarketLiquid: agent 0.126, market 0.111 (weight 0.67), blend 0.106.
limits: Simplex regression, leave-one-out, bootstrap 1000.
agent_relevance: Blend a model with an outside signal using fitted weights, not equal weights.

source: Neyman and Roughgarden (2022) Are You Smarter Than a Random Expert
finding: Theory: when experts' signals are substitutes, the average beats a random expert. With a known prior, extremizing the average by a factor d from the prior is the worst-case optimal move.
numbers: d rises with the number of experts k and tops out at sqrt(3), about 1.732. Guarantee about 2.598/k. Plain averaging (d=1) has a weaker guarantee.
quote: extremizing the average by moving it away from the prior by a constant factor
limits: Needs the projective-substitutes condition. Complementary signals break the result.
agent_relevance: Same-model samples are strong substitutes. That supports a mild push (d up to about 1.7) at most.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Universal Self-Consistency
finding: Asking an LLM to pick the most consistent of its own sampled answers matches majority-vote self-consistency and works on open-ended text.
numbers: Reported to match standard self-consistency on math reasoning and to help on code and summarization (abstract level). No forecast numbers.
limits: LLM-as-aggregator. In c06 the USC variant did worse than the mean on forecasting (0.1691 vs 0.1656).
agent_relevance: Fine for text answers. For probabilities use a numeric rule.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought
finding: Sampling many reasoning paths and taking the most common final answer beat greedy chain of thought.
numbers: Absolute gains: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9 points.
limits: Needs matchable answers. Votes from one model share biases, so gains are bounded.
agent_relevance: The origin of majority-vote aggregation in an LLM loop. Votes, not extremizing.

source: Li et al. (2024) More Agents Is All You Need (Agent Forest)
finding: Sampling and voting gets better with more agents, and small models can beat big ones.
numbers: GSM8K gains 12 to 24 points, MATH 6 to 10, MMLU 5 to 11, Chess 1 to 4, HumanEval 4 to 9. Llama2-13B ensemble 59% on GSM8K vs Llama2-70B 54%. Gains rise then taper at the hardest setting (inherent difficulty 400).
limits: Cost grows linearly in agents.
agent_relevance: Voting shrinks random error but cannot fix a systematic one.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency (CISC)
finding: Weighting each vote by the model's own confidence reaches the same accuracy with fewer samples.
numbers: Nine models, four datasets. Over 40% fewer reasoning paths on average; 73% fewer in the best case (Gemma2-9B on MATH).
limits: Needs a usable confidence signal, ranking within a question only.
agent_relevance: A weighted pool beats an equal pool in the LLM setting too, as with performance-weighted human pooling.

source: Debate or Vote (2025) majority voting explains multi-agent debate gains
finding: Majority voting alone reproduces most of the gain of multi-agent debate. In their model debate is a martingale on beliefs, so debate alone does not raise expected correctness.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B average over 7 tasks: single agent 0.7205, decentralized debate 0.7377 (T=2), majority voting 0.7691; centralized debate 0.655 to 0.667. Llama3.1-8B single 0.6203, debate about 0.68 to 0.70.
limits: Small open models, 7 NLP benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Do not buy debate rounds to get an aggregation gain. Independent samples plus a vote do as well.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty
finding: Verbalized confidence is overconfident. Consistency over samples and better aggregation reduce this, but no method wins everywhere.
numbers: Five datasets, five LLMs including GPT-4 and LLaMA 2 Chat. Black-box vs white-box AUROC gap narrow: 0.522 vs 0.605.
limits: Hard tasks (professional knowledge) stay poor.
agent_relevance: Raw model confidence is already too high. Pushing it outward compounds the problem (G4).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Mixture-of-Agents
finding: Layers of LLM agents that read each other's answers beat GPT-4 Omni on instruction benchmarks.
numbers: AlpacaEval 2.0: MoA with open models 65.1% vs GPT-4 Omni 57.5%.
limits: Open-ended chat quality, not probabilities. Agents see peers' answers, so they are not independent.
agent_relevance: A layered synthesis design exists, but its evidence is about text, not calibrated forecasts.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on Real-World Forecasting Against Expert Forecasters
finding: On 464 Metaculus questions, o3 beat a reference crowd Brier but not the expert group. Mean and median over 5 samples gave nearly the same score.
numbers: o3: median ensemble 0.1352 (SE 0.0097), mean 0.1362; GPT-4.1 0.1542 vs 0.1509; GPT-4o 0.1883 vs 0.1851. References: crowd 0.149 (Halawi), 0.121 (Karger).
limits: Cross-study Brier not comparable. Five samples averaged per question.
agent_relevance: Mean vs median over same-model samples does not matter. Reasoning models score best.

source: Schoenegger, Jones et al. (2025) Prompt Engineering LLM Forecasting
finding: Across 38 prompts and four models, most prompt tweaks gave tiny gains. Base-rate prompts helped slightly. Bayesian-reasoning prompts hurt.
numbers: 38 prompts in Study 1, plus compound prompts and o1 models in Study 2. Superforecasting persona (short) difference -0.001 Brier, p=0.93. Bayesian reasoning and Propose-Evaluate-Select significantly worse.
limits: Not an aggregation study.
agent_relevance: A persona prompt will not fix calibration. Fix it after the fact with a fitted map.

source: Prophet Arena (2025) prompt ensembles and self-consistency for forecasts
finding: Averaging forecasts from several prompt variants did not help, since the model gives nearly the same number each time. Counting yes/no samples was clearly worse.
numbers: Brier/ECE GPT-5: default 0.165/0.020, ensemble 0.160/0.024. Grok 4: default 0.186, ensemble 0.177. Unweighted self-consistency Brier 0.231 to 0.267 across five models.
limits: Prompt variants differ by less than 0.01 Brier. Counting 10 yes/no answers gives coarse probabilities.
agent_relevance: Sample ensembling of one model brings little diversity, so independence cannot justify extremizing.

source: Turtel et al. (2025) Outcome-based RL to Predict the Future
finding: A 14B model trained with outcome RL, with 7-run ensembling, beat o1 on Brier and calibration. Plain training drifted to extreme overconfidence unless guarded.
numbers: 1,265 test questions: ensemble-7 Brier 0.190, ECE 0.062; single ReMax 0.199; base R1-14B 0.215; o1 0.202; market better by 0.039. Simulated Polymarket profit about 52 dollars.
limits: Market still better. Polymarket questions only.
agent_relevance: Models drift toward extreme outputs on their own, so a push outward is risky.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
finding: Evaluation advice: a system that retrieves the market crowd forecast can look good without skill. Benchmarks should measure edge over the crowd.
numbers: No headline figure; position and analysis paper.
limits: Only the crowd-aggregate section was read closely.
agent_relevance: Test any aggregation or extremizing step on resolved questions after the model cutoff.
